extracted.intended_audience: editors, literary critics, scholars, and informed readers of biography and textual editions
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative standards and best practices for preparing, annotating, and publishing scholarly editions of life/biographical works (preserving original text, annotation practice, factual accuracy, and classical scholarship).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual accuracy of dates and events
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements of dates, lifespans, and chronological facts must be correct (e.g., years of birth/death, dates of publication, dates of military surrenders and executions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review documents many concrete errors (Allan Ramsay dates; Lord Mansfield surviving Johnson 'full ten years' when it was eight years and a quarter; General Burgoyne's surrender given as March 1778 instead of 17 Oct 1777; Byng's trial and execution administration timeline). Such mistakes show 'no adequate sense of the obligation which a writer, who professes to relate facts, owes to the public.' Verify against common reference works/primary sources before asserting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency and internal coherence of biographical assertions
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid making contradictory statements about the same person or event within the work (e.g., giving multiple incompatible ages or dates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Mr. Croker provides three different statements about Mrs. Thrale’s age; two of the three must be incorrect. An editor should check internal consistency and resolve contradictions rather than leaving mutually incompatible claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify citations and authorities (consult primary sources)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on secondary or misread authorities; read the primary or cited source closely before summarizing or asserting its content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The editor asserts about the History of Prince Titi without properly reading Park’s Royal and Noble Authors, which shows the manuscript was given up to the Government. The advice: take the trouble to read the passages you cite with attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve the original author's text and voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Reprint the original narrative precisely as the author wrote it; do not alter phrasing, tone, or structure of the original work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic insists Mr. Croker should have reprinted Boswell’s narrative exactly and relegated additions to notes or appendices. 'We love...to read the great productions of the human mind as they were written.' Avoid 'rifacimenti, harmonies, abridgments, expurgated editions.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not intersperse other writers' extracts into the main text
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotations or extracts from other authors should be placed in notes or appendices, not inserted into the primary narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: 'An editor might as well publish Thucydides with extracts from Diodorus interspersed.' Croker's practice of inserting Mrs. Thrale, Hawkins, Tyers, Murphy, etc., into Boswell's text disrupts unity and is condemned; such material should be clearly separated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respectful and consistent handling of indecorous material
rubrics_metrics.description: If expurgation is performed, apply it systematically and transparently; do not capriciously omit some indecorous passages while leaving others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Croker's 'prudery' is called 'capricious'—one faint allusion omitted, another coarse jest retained. The editor should be consistent in policy and mindful of how selective censorship distorts the original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notes should add substantive value, not trivial commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotations must provide meaningful information, clarification, or scholarship rather than the 'flattest and poorest reflections' accessible to any casual reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic finds many of Croker's 2,500 notes are banal observations that interrupt the narrative. Notes should illuminate the text, not state the obvious or belabor commonplaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate classical and philological scholarship
rubrics_metrics.description: When commenting on classical texts, phrases, or authors (Latin/Greek), the editor must demonstrate competence or consult competent authorities before pronouncing judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Croker's mistakes about Juvenal, Horace, 'Lucina', philarchus/phylarchus, and corrupt readings of Euripides show the danger of authoritative commentary without competence. When in doubt, consult recognized scholars (example invoked: Sir Robert Peel) or refrain from overconfident judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct translation and interpretation of Latin and Greek passages
rubrics_metrics.description: Translations and glosses of foreign-language passages must be linguistically accurate and not strained conjectures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: mistranslating 'Si per te licet, imperatur nuncio Holderum ad me deducere' or misreading 'th ph' as 'phnetoi philoi.' Editors should prefer conservative readings or state emendations transparently, and study classical references (Corderius suggested as remedial study).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bibliographical accuracy (publication dates and edition history)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure correct publication years and edition facts for works cited or discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Croker misdates Goldsmith’s Vicar of Wakefield (given as 1761; actually 1766) and confuses when parts of Gibbon were written/published. Editors should check bibliographies and primary editions rather than rely on memory or hearsay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful proofreading and printing accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid typesetting errors, solecisms, and printer's blunders in both text and notes; ensure the printed edition is clean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewer blames both editor and printer for grammatical solecisms and misprints. A responsible edition requires rigorous copy-editing and proofreading to prevent 'all sorts of blunders.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear attribution and editorial transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Make it evident which passages are the original author's and which are editorial insertions or quotations from other writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Croker's insertions force readers to 'keep his eye on the margin' to see the source of each passage. Editors should label insertions clearly (notes, appendices) so the reader can follow authorship without confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary modernization or paraphrase of classic texts
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not 'modernize' or paraphrase older works in a way that loses their distinctive diction and character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay decries modernizing transformations (e.g., 'Mr. Gilpin’s translation of John Bunyan' or altering Milton) that remove the original flavor. Preserve historical diction unless a separate modernized edition is explicitly offered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select quotations and supplementary material according to the original author's taste
rubrics_metrics.description: If incorporating material from other sources, choose and introduce selections as the original author would have done to preserve cohesion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic notes Croker's borrowed passages are 'not chosen as Boswell would have chosen them... not introduced as Boswell would have introduced them.' Editors should exercise curatorial sympathy with the original writer's approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly humility: avoid authoritative pronouncements without evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not make confident corrections or decisive-sounding claims when evidence is lacking; avoid 'cool and authoritative' assertions that are unsupported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review repeatedly faults Croker for confident but false statements. An editor’s duty to the public requires caution and checking; negligent authority is worse than modest uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness in criticizing others' accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: When correcting prior accounts or biographies, ensure your own corrections are accurate and defensible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Croker reproaches others for inaccuracy while committing larger errors himself; editors should not correct unless they have verified the correction thoroughly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid trivializing or over-interpreting plain language
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not invent obscurities where the text is plain or misread clear idioms and conceits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: misreading Sir William Jones's couplet and missing the conceit that 'all' substitutes for 'one'; miscalling obvious jokes or conceits 'not quite clear.' Proofreaders and editors should not manufacture difficulties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain the unity and integrity of the work
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not fragment or 'dovetail' the book with unrelated insertions; preserve the single-minded effect of an original work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewer argues that Boswell's Life is 'one great entire work' whose character is harmed by interpolations. Editors should respect that unity—use appendices/notes rather than integrating foreign material into the body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use precise genealogical and titular forms appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow conventions for names/titles in genealogical contexts vs polished literary usage (inflect where appropriate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Johnson's comment about giving 'inflection' to names in elegant prose is cited. Editors should use bare names in genealogical lists but inflected/grammatical forms in running literary prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist petty, needless commentary and the commentator’s ego
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotations should not be a vehicle for the editor’s petty judgments or gratuitous moralizing about the author's habits/personality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic complains that Croker stops the narrative to remark on Johnson's rudeness, port-wine taste, Boswell's impertinence, etc., which are trivial and interruptive. Keep editorial voice restrained and relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about editorial alterations
rubrics_metrics.description: When altering a paragraph or removing an inaccuracy, declare it transparently in editorial notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text includes a parenthetical: '[This paragraph has been altered; and a slight inaccuracy immaterial to the argument, has been removed.]'. Such transparency is good practice and should be used consistently when making emendations.
